explanation: Tolkien fell for Finnish after finding a Finnish grammar as a student. His other main Elvish tongue, Sindarin, was shaped to sound like Welsh.

claims.text: Tolkien said that Finnish strongly shaped the sound and structure of his Elvish language Quenya.
Tolkien did not name Welsh, Irish or Hungarian as the inspiration for Quenya.
As a student, Tolkien discovered a Finnish grammar and was delighted by the language.
Sindarin, another of Tolkien's Elvish languages, was modelled on the sound of Welsh.

writerNotes: Welsh is the expert's trap, because it shaped Sindarin, the other Elvish language. Tolkien also named Latin and Greek as ingredients of Quenya, so neither appears among the options. Self-check (9.3): lint run clean; every claim listed with risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where honest; datasets: no pinned dataset covers it; rival test: Welsh is right for Sindarin, not Quenya; Irish and Hungarian were never named as the base; volatility evergreen, no time words, nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026; regional: Tolkien's books and films are known worldwide; style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes, explanation within 35 words; myths: no match in myths.json; mystery and encore checks: not applicable to a practice item; doubts: the stem paraphrases Tolkien's letters rather than quoting them, so it does not depend on exact wording

evidence.restatement: Tolkien wrote in his letters that Finnish was the dominant influence on the sound and structure of Quenya.

Tolkien said his invented languages became heavily Finnish in phonetic pattern and structure after he met a Finnish grammar (a lecture of 1955 and letters), and he named Finnish as Quenya's model.

claimResults.note: Rival test: Welsh is the trap, because Tolkien tied it to Sindarin. He also called Quenya Latin-based with Finnish and Greek flavours, but Latin and Greek are not options.
